questions.q: Inside a nucleus the positive protons repel each other by the electrostatic force, yet the nucleus stays together. Which force overcomes that repulsion and holds the nucleons together?
options: The strong nuclear force
The gravitational force between the nucleons
The weak nuclear force
The electrostatic force between the protons
questions.explanation: Two protons do repel each other, but in the nucleus they are so close that the repulsion is overcome by an even stronger force — the strong nuclear force. It is very strong but acts over only incredibly small distances, so the nucleons must be close together for it to dominate.

questions.q: As the number of protons in a nucleus increases, why are more neutrons needed to maintain nuclear stability?
options: Neutrons have no charge, so they share the strong nuclear force without adding to the cumulative repulsion of the protons
Neutrons increase the electrostatic repulsion that binds the nucleus together
Neutrons cancel the positive charge of the protons, making the nucleus neutral
Extra neutrons increase the gravitational attraction between the nucleons
questions.explanation: In larger nuclei the cumulative repulsion of the protons makes the nucleus less stable. Neutrons do not have a charge and so do not add to that repulsion, but they do still share the strong nuclear force, so larger nuclei need more neutrons than protons to stay stable.

questions.q: Which list orders alpha, beta and gamma radiation correctly from lowest to highest penetrating power?
options: Alpha, beta, gamma
Gamma, beta, alpha
Beta, alpha, gamma
Alpha, gamma, beta
questions.explanation: Penetrating power is lowest for alpha particles, which can be stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta particles are stopped by about a centimetre of aluminium, while gamma rays may pass through a few centimetres of lead or many metres of concrete before being stopped.

questions.q: According to the summary of radiation properties, what is the nature of beta radiation and how does its path behave through a magnetic field?
options: An electron that follows a curved path of negative charge
A helium nucleus that follows a curved path of positive charge
A high energy photon that is not deflected
A neutron that follows a straight, undeflected path
questions.explanation: The summary table identifies beta radiation as an electron, with moderate ionising power and high penetrating power, that follows a curved path of negative charge through a magnetic field. Alpha is a positively charged helium nucleus and gamma is an undeflected high energy photon.

questions.q: In any nuclear reaction written in the form A-Z-X, which quantities must balance (sum to the same value) on both sides of the equation?
options: The mass number and the atomic number must each balance on both sides
Only the mass number must balance
Only the atomic number must balance
The total mass in kilograms must be identical on both sides
questions.explanation: In any nuclear reaction the sum of the mass numbers before the reaction must equal the sum of the mass numbers after, and the sum of the atomic numbers before must likewise equal the sum after. For beta decay the emitted electron is assigned an atomic number of negative 1.

questions.q: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) undergoes alpha decay. Determine the mass number of the daughter thorium nucleus.
questions.given: Parent uranium-238: mass number A = 238, atomic number Z = 92; emits an alpha particle (helium-4 nucleus)
working: Alpha decay reduces the mass number by four and the atomic number by two.
Atomic number of daughter \(= 92 - 2 = 90\), which is thorium.
questions.explanation: Alpha decay reduces the atomic number by two and the mass number by four, giving the textbook equation U-238 to Th-234 plus helium-4. Always show the check that the mass numbers and atomic numbers balance on each side.

questions.q: Uranium-238 decays through a series of steps until it reaches the stable isotope lead-206. Given that only alpha decay changes the mass number, and each alpha decay reduces it by four, how many alpha decays occur in this decay series?
questions.given: Start: uranium-238 (mass number 238). End: stable lead-206 (mass number 206). Each alpha decay reduces the mass number by 4.
working: Only alpha decay reduces the mass number; beta decay leaves it unchanged.
questions.explanation: As alpha decay is the only decay that reduces the mass number, and each alpha decay decreases it by four, the uranium-238 series to lead-206 must involve (238 − 206)/4 = 8 alpha decays. The accompanying drop in atomic number is then made up by six beta decays.

questions.q: From memory: using the strong nuclear force and the electrostatic repulsion of protons, explain why larger nuclei need more neutrons than protons to remain stable.
keyPoints: In larger nuclei the cumulative repulsion of the protons makes the nucleus less stable.
Neutrons do not have a charge, so they do not add to that repulsion, but they do still share the strong nuclear force.
Hence larger nuclei need progressively more neutrons than protons, an increasing trend as the number of protons grows.
questions.explanation: If you named the cumulative proton repulsion, the chargeless neutron adding strong-force attraction without repulsion, and the resulting neutron excess for big nuclei, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: why did physicists propose the (anti)neutrino, a particle they could not detect, to explain beta decay?
keyPoints: Beta particles are emitted with a continuous range of energies, not the single sharp value seen in alpha decay, so energy and momentum appeared not to balance.
Rather than abandon the conservation of energy and momentum, Pauli (1930) proposed an extra neutral, near-massless particle to carry away the missing energy and momentum.
Fermi named it the neutrino and built it into his theory; the neutrino itself was not directly detected until 1956.
questions.explanation: The key move is: don't throw away conservation laws — instead predict the invisible particle that saves them. This mirrors the reasoning that led to the neutron. Grade Good if you linked the continuous beta spectrum to conservation and Pauli's proposal.

questions.q: Describe the role of the weak nuclear force in beta-minus decay at the level of quarks. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: In beta-minus decay the weak nuclear force, carried by the W boson, converts a down quark into an up quark inside a neutron. This changes the neutron (up-down-down) into a proton (up-up-down), and emits an electron — the beta particle — together with an electron antineutrino. The proton remains in the nucleus, so the atomic number rises by one while the mass number is unchanged.

criteria.descriptor: Names the weak nuclear force (carried by the W boson) and the quark flavour change: a down quark becomes an up quark.
States this turns the neutron into a proton, emitting an electron (beta particle) and an electron antineutrino.
Notes the atomic number increases by one while the mass number stays the same.

questions.explanation: Full marks require naming the force and W boson, the down-to-up quark change, the emitted beta particle and antineutrino, and the effect on the atomic number.
